definition.text: Aquaculture, or aquafarming, is the controlled farming of aquatic organisms such as fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and aquatic plants.

facts.text: It raises freshwater, brackish and saltwater populations under controlled conditions, unlike commercial fishing, which harvests wild fish.
Stagnant wild harvests and growing demand for protein pushed farmers to domesticate more marine species, raising hopes of a 'Blue Revolution'.
With capture production static since the late 1980s, aquaculture has supplied the continuing growth in fish for human consumption.
In 2016 aquaculture made up 47 percent of the 171 million tonnes of fish produced, and in 2014 farmed fish overtook wild fish as human food.
Farming carnivorous fish like salmon does not relieve wild stocks because they are fed fishmeal and fish oil from wild forage fish.
Shrimp farming helped destroy about 20 percent of mangrove forests since 1980, and a 200,000-salmon farm discharges more faecal waste than a city of 60,000.
Shellfish farming adds filter-feeding capacity that can significantly improve water quality.
Farming creates private stocks, giving farmers a reason to conserve them.

definition.text: Integrated multi-trophic aquaculture recycles the wastes of one farmed species as food or fertiliser for another.

facts.text: Fed species such as fish or shrimp are combined with extractive species such as shellfish to balance the system environmentally and economically.
Bivalves like oysters and mussels feed on the surrounding natural production rather than added feed, so shellfish farming is usually seen as benign.

definition.text: The Beverton–Holt model is a classic discrete-time population model that predicts next generation's numbers from this generation's, levelling off at carrying capacity.

facts.text: Ray Beverton and Sidney Holt introduced it for fisheries in 1957.
Their 1957 work on North Sea fisheries became the theoretical basis of North European management in the 1960s.
It is the discrete-time counterpart of the logistic growth equation, and can be solved exactly.
The Ricker model generalises it to include scramble competition.

definition.text: Bycatch is fish or other marine life caught unintentionally while fishing for particular species or sizes.

facts.text: It may be the wrong species, the wrong sex, or undersized young of the target species.
Bycatch is about a quarter of all marine catch and is usually thrown back to die.
Shrimp trawls take two percent of the world's catch by weight but produce over one-third of all bycatch.
Gillnets, longlines and bottom trawls cause most bycatch, which includes dolphins, sea turtles and seabirds.
An estimated 100,000 albatross a year are killed on longlines.
Remedies include closing areas with high bycatch and changing fishing gear.
Norway's 'no discards' policy makes fishers keep everything they catch.

definition.text: Bycatch reduction devices and other gear changes let unwanted animals escape from fishing gear.

facts.text: Turtle excluder devices use a grid that deflects turtles out of a trawl net through an opening.
Approved US devices cut finfish bycatch by 30%, though surveys suggest they work less well than thought.
Designing gear to be more selective is called conservation engineering; bigger mesh openings let small fish escape.
Streamer lines cut seabird deaths in Alaskan longline fisheries by about 70%.
